metadata.title: Trends in international assessments and outcomes in adulthood

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study constructs cohort-by-country-by-survey-year cells by linking adolescent test scores from PISA 2018 (math) and TIMSS 2019 (Grade 8 math) to adult outcomes from PIAAC (numeracy) and harmonized Survey Data Recycling (SDR) sources. For PIAAC-based regressions, the author normalizes individual sampling weights within each country-by-survey-year cell and then uses the sum of normalized weights as the cell weight. For SDR-based regressions, the author weights each cell using the sum of SDR-provided weights, rescaling national survey weights so that the sum within each survey equals the number of respondents. Standard errors are clustered by country and birth year; the manuscript does not report replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight inference is not documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not use plausible values (PVs) for cognitive achievement in the sense of ILSA PV-based scoring; instead, it rescales PISA and TIMSS scores to a common metric and then aggregates to country-by-birth-cohort averages. Missing-data handling is described for cohort-score imputation (assigning the closest non-missing test score within two birth years) and for dropping observations with inconsistent age reporting, but the paper does not provide a general, explicit missing-data strategy for all variables in the regression models (e.g., whether listwise deletion or multiple imputation was used for each outcome). This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling beyond the described cohort-score imputation rules.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis is built at the cohort-by-country-by-survey-year level by (i) restricting PISA to students in the modal grade for their country and restricting TIMSS to students within a 1-year range centered on the modal age, (ii) rescaling TIMSS Grade 8 math scores to the PISA math scale using conversion parameters estimated in common linking countries (countries participating in both TIMSS 2019 and PISA 2018), (iii) computing average birth year and average math test score per country and testing round, (iv) imputing missing cohort test-score observations by assigning the closest non-missing test score no more than two birth years away (ties resolved by taking the later test score), (v) keeping only country-by-cohort observations that have both PISA and TIMSS scores, and (vi) restricting the SDR-linked sample to respondents aged 16+ with non-missing PISA and TIMSS cohort scores; additionally, dropping observations where the difference between predicted age (survey year minus birth year) and reported age exceeds 2. For PIAAC, the author collapses individual numeracy scores to country-by-cohort-by-survey-year averages and links them to the cohort’s rescaled PISA/TIMSS scores by country and birth year.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012/2014/2017 (adult numeracy), linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS 2015/2019 Grade 8 math (cohort-by-country averages)
top_predictors: TIMSS (Grade 8, PISA scale) math score (cohort average)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 2: PISA coefficient 0.198 (SE 0.090), p<0.05 in Column 1; TIMSS coefficient 0.221 (SE 0.104), p<0.05 in Column 2. R² ≈ 0.938–0.945 across specifications. Equality test PISA = TIMSS: p=0.686 (Column 2) and p=0.879 (Column 5).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012/2014/2017 numeracy data linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (rescaled to the PISA scale) at the country-by-birth-cohort level, the study leveraged cohort-average PISA and TIMSS math scores to predict cohort-average adult numeracy, finding that both PISA and TIMSS scores are positively associated with adult numeracy (about 0.20–0.22 SD higher numeracy per 1 SD higher adolescent math). This indicates that adolescent math proficiency, regardless of whether it is measured via PISA or TIMSS, is strongly related to later-life numeracy skills, though the paper emphasizes these are associations rather than causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: SDR harmonized adult education outcomes linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (cohort-by-country averages)
top_predictors: TIMSS (Grade 8, PISA scale) math score (cohort average)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 Panel A: PISA coefficients 0.739 (SE 0.345), p<0.05 in Column 1; 0.715 (SE 0.335), p<0.05 in Column 2; 0.540 (SE 0.423) not significant in Column 3. TIMSS coefficients 0.236 (SE 0.194) not significant in Column 1; 0.125 (SE 0.122) not significant in Column 2; −0.005 (SE 0.246) not significant in Column 5. R² ≈ 0.744–0.945 depending on specification. Equality test PISA = TIMSS: p=0.091 (Column 2) and p=0.023 (Column 8).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using SDR harmonized adult education data linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (rescaled to the PISA scale) at the country-by-birth-cohort level, the study leveraged cohort-average PISA and TIMSS math scores to predict adult years of education, finding that PISA scores show a consistently positive and often statistically significant association (roughly 0.5–1.0 additional years per 1 SD higher adolescent math), while TIMSS scores are small and generally not significant. This indicates that PISA-measured math performance may be more informative for forecasting later educational attainment than TIMSS in this cohort-level framework, suggesting caution when harmonizing “human capital” across testing regimes.

main_findings.dataset_used: SDR harmonized adult education outcomes linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (cohort-by-country averages)
top_predictors: TIMSS (Grade 8, PISA scale) math score (cohort average)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 Panel B: PISA coefficients 0.122 (SE 0.054), p<0.05 in Column 1; 0.118 (SE 0.051), p<0.05 in Column 2; 0.108 (SE 0.058) p<0.1 in Column 3. TIMSS coefficients 0.045 (SE 0.050) not significant in Column 1; 0.032 (SE 0.039) not significant in Column 2; 0.003 (SE 0.029) not significant in Column 6. R² ≈ 0.507–0.768. Equality test PISA = TIMSS: p=0.181 (Column 2) and p=0.027 (Column 8).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using SDR harmonized adult education data linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (rescaled to the PISA scale) at the country-by-birth-cohort level, the study leveraged cohort-average PISA and TIMSS math scores to predict secondary school completion, finding that higher PISA scores are associated with higher secondary completion rates (about 10–12 percentage points per 1 SD), whereas TIMSS scores show no systematic relationship. This indicates that PISA-based monitoring of math may better flag cohorts at risk of lower secondary attainment, informing targeted education policy and research on why the two assessment regimes differ in predictive strength.

main_findings.dataset_used: SDR harmonized adult education outcomes linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (cohort-by-country averages)
top_predictors: TIMSS (Grade 8, PISA scale) math score (cohort average)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 Panel C: PISA coefficients −0.071 (SE 0.063) not significant in Column 1; −0.062 (SE 0.062) not significant in Column 3; 0.013 (SE 0.037) not significant in Column 5. TIMSS coefficients 0.046 (SE 0.024) p<0.1 in Column 1; 0.046 (SE 0.031) not significant in Column 3; 0.025 (SE 0.024) not significant in Column 5. R² ≈ 0.567–0.801. Equality test PISA = TIMSS: p=0.112 (Column 2) and p=0.719 (Column 8).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using SDR harmonized adult education data linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (rescaled to the PISA scale) at the country-by-birth-cohort level, the study leveraged cohort-average PISA and TIMSS math scores to predict bachelor’s completion, finding no clear or consistently significant relationship for either assessment (effects are imprecise and often not statistically significant). This indicates that cohort-level math proficiency measured in adolescence may be less predictive of tertiary completion than of secondary completion, implying that additional mechanisms (e.g., access constraints, tracking, and labor-market pathways) likely mediate bachelor’s attainment.

main_findings.dataset_used: SDR harmonized adult income outcomes linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (cohort-by-country averages)
top_predictors: TIMSS (Grade 8, PISA scale) math score (cohort average)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 3 Panel D: PISA coefficients 7.470 (SE 2.357), p<0.01 in Column 1; 7.608 (SE 2.334), p<0.01 in Column 2; 12.127 (SE 3.684), p<0.01 in Column 5; 11.749 (SE 3.572), p<0.01 in Column 6. TIMSS coefficients 3.908 (SE 1.312), p<0.05 in Column 1; 4.031 (SE 1.494), p<0.05 in Column 2; 3.465 (SE 1.578), p<0.1 in Column 8. R² ≈ 0.565–0.716. Equality test PISA = TIMSS: p=0.256 (Column 2) and p=0.027 (Column 8).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using SDR harmonized adult income data linked to PISA 2018 math and TIMSS Grade 8 math (rescaled to the PISA scale) at the country-by-birth-cohort level, the study leveraged cohort-average PISA and TIMSS math scores to predict household income percentile, finding that higher PISA scores are associated with substantially higher adult income percentiles (about 7–12 percentile points per 1 SD), while TIMSS scores show smaller but still positive and sometimes significant effects (about 3–4 percentile points per 1 SD). This indicates that PISA-measured math performance may be more strongly connected to later economic outcomes, supporting policy attention to improving PISA-relevant math skills while recognizing the estimates are associations rather than causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The paper links adolescent math performance from PISA (math, age-based sample; PISA 2018 used for the linking scale) and TIMSS (Grade 8 math; TIMSS 2019 used for linking) to adult outcomes from PIAAC numeracy (2012/2014/2017) and harmonized SDR education and income measures. Scores are rescaled to a common PISA scale and then aggregated to country-by-birth-cohort averages; missing cohort test-score observations are imputed using the closest non-missing score within two birth years. In PIAAC, both PISA and TIMSS cohort math scores are positively associated with adult numeracy (Table 2: coefficients around 0.20–0.22 SD per 1 SD higher adolescent math; R² ≈ 0.94). In SDR outcomes, PISA shows stronger and more consistent associations with years of education and secondary completion, while bachelor’s completion shows no clear relationship; for income, PISA effects are larger (about 7–12 percentile points) than TIMSS (about 3–4). The study reports robust standard errors clustered by country and birth year and uses fixed effects, but it explicitly cautions that the estimates are associations, not causal effects.
